one_liner: Go assembly (avo-generated AVX2) kernels for ASCII case-folding, byte swapping, fixed-size-key sort and base64; 6-13x over the package's pure-Go fallbacks.
what_it_does: A set of small Go packages (ascii, base64, bswap, mem, qsort, slices, sortedset, utf8, keyset) whose functions work on whole byte arrays: ascii.EqualFold/EqualFoldString, bswap.Swap64 (in-place big-to-little-endian over 8-byte items), qsort.Sort(data, size, swap) for packed 8/16/24/32-byte big-endian keys, and a base64 Encoding that mirrors encoding/base64. Each function has a Go fallback picked automatically on platforms without assembly, or forced with the purego build tag. APIs resemble the stdlib but are not drop-in: qsort sorts raw byte buffers, not sort.Interface, and ascii folds ASCII only.
how_it_is_fast: EqualFoldString compares 128 bytes per loop with AVX2: it XORs the two inputs, builds a mask of positions where the byte is a letter and differs only in bit 0x20, and checks with one VPMOVMSKB per block, finishing with an overlapping 16-byte tail load. Swap64 uses VPSHUFB over four 32-byte registers per iteration. qsort byte-swaps the buffer once so keys compare as native qwords, then runs a quicksort whose partition is the branchless hybrid Lomuto/Hoare 'distribute' scheme from the reverberate.org bubble-sort post (CMOV plus VPCMPEQQ/VPCMPGTQ over 1 KB of stack scratch), finishing runs of 16-32 items with a branchless two-at-a-time bubble sort (8-byte keys) or an assembly insertion sort (16 and 32-byte keys).
when_to_use: Go services on amd64 with AVX2 that compare many ASCII header names, keys or tokens case-insensitively, at 16 bytes or more per string
Converting large big-endian arrays of uint64 (wire formats, Parquet/Arrow-style columns) to little-endian in place
Sorting millions of fixed-width binary keys (8, 16 or 32-byte IDs, UUIDs, hashes) stored contiguously in a []byte, by memcmp order, with no swap callback
Hot paths where the inputs are batches of values, since the README says the functions are built for arrays
when_not_to_use: Unicode text: ascii.EqualFold compares non-ASCII bytes exactly, so it disagrees with strings.EqualFold on UTF-8 case pairs
arm64 or other non-amd64 targets for ascii, bswap and qsort: these packages have amd64 assembly only and fall back to Go (base64 does have arm64 assembly)
Short strings or single small calls: below 16 bytes EqualFoldString uses its scalar table path, and Go assembly functions are never inlined
Adversarial or untrusted sort input: qsort is plain median-of-three quicksort with no heapsort fallback, so it is quadratic in the worst case
Projects that need active maintenance or support for current Go releases: code last changed May 2022 and CI ran only Go 1.17 and 1.18

integration.dependencies: golang.org/x/sys (CPU feature detection); avo only in the separate build module for regenerating assembly
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.17+ (go.mod says go 1.18; v1.1.5 is the last release for Go 1.16)
integration.platforms: amd64 with runtime AVX2/AVX/CMOV dispatch for ascii, bswap and qsort; base64 also has arm64 assembly; any other platform uses the pure-Go fallback
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the functions keep no state, but qsort.Sort and bswap.Swap64 rewrite the caller's buffer in place (Sort byte-swaps the whole buffer and swaps it back at the end)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — ascii.EqualFoldString has the strings.EqualFold signature but ASCII-only semantics; base64 mirrors encoding/base64 but only accepts the standard, URL and IMAP alphabets; qsort and bswap have no stdlib equivalent with the same interface

gotchas: Builds with GO111MODULE=off or some vendored/GOPATH setups fail to link with "undefined reference to github.com/segmentio/asm/cpu.X86" (issues #73 and #81, both open); turning modules on or building with -tags purego avoids it.

The showcase GB/s figures are inflated by the harness: BenchmarkEqualFoldString calls SetBytes(len(lower)+len(upper)), so 49.44 GB/s counts both 512-byte inputs (about 24.7 GB/s per string); Swap64 runs in place on a 64 KiB buffer that stays in L2, so 73.67 GB/s is cache bandwidth, not memory bandwidth. The time ratios are unaffected.

The sort benchmarks have more broken rows than the verifier listed: stdlibSort8PartiallySorted allocates make([]int64, size) and then appends the partitions, so copy(data, partiallyOrdered) copies only the zero-filled prefix and the 'partially-sorted' sort.Slice rows sort an all-zero array; the dead partiallyOrdered branch of benchSort fills nothing, sorts each partition as a single element and appends it after the random prefix that copy() actually uses; stdlibSort8 draws keys from [0, size/10) as signed int64, unlike the random bytes BenchmarkSort8 sorts, so the two are not comparable even if published. BenchmarkSort32 (size 0) measures nothing.

qsort.Sort sorts big-endian byte order, panics if len(data) is not a multiple of size, and drops to the slower Hoare partition whenever a swap callback is passed (the hybrid assembly path needs swap == nil); sizes other than 8, 16, 24 and 32 fall back to sort.Sort with bytes.Compare.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: vek, kelindar/simd and tphakala/simd target numeric float/int vector math in Go; pick segmentio/asm when the hot path is byte-level work such as ASCII case-insensitive comparison, endian swapping, sorting packed fixed-width binary keys or base64.
verified_claims_summary: A first-party benchstat snapshot (2021, i9-8950HK, macOS amd64, Go version not stated, n=5) compares each function's assembly build against the same package built with -tags purego: EqualFoldString on 512-byte equal strings 276 ns to 21 ns (about 13x), Swap64 on a 64 KiB buffer 11.2 us to 0.9 us (about 12.6x), and Sort16 on 1,000,000 random 16-byte keys 269 ms to 46 ms (about 5.8x). No Go standard library function (strings.EqualFold, sort.Slice) appears in the published numbers, and the Sort16 gain also comes from a different partition algorithm and the AVX2 byte-swap passes, not only from SIMD compares.
status_note: Stale: code last changed May 2022, the last commit (Nov 2023, v1.2.1) only relicensed MIT to MIT-0, and 9 issues are open including the cpu.X86 link failure; small, permissively licensed (MIT-0, no patent grant) and pulled in transitively by large Go projects (issue #73 cites a vendored Grafana 8.5 build), so still usable as a dependency or vendored source.
